The CO, Acceptor Process would produce somewhat different stack emissions, compared to the Lurgi process. These emissions would come from the dolomite-recalcining unit. Particulate matter in the exhaust would be lower, since coal char (containing less ash than coal) would be burned. Oxides of nitrogen would cause a greater problem, but the controls used for other types of burners can be used in the recalcining operations. However, the concentration of SO, in the exhaust from the recalcining process is much greater than for normal coal burning. The reason for this is that the dolomite in the various units absorbs H2S prior to the recalcining process. While most of the H2S is reclaimed, enough sulfur remains to cause SO2 problems when the dolomite is recalcining. Scrubbers with SO<sub>2</sub> removal efficiencies approaching 90 percent would have to be perfected before emissions could meet EPA standards. (Manufacturers presently claim these efficiencies for their products, but to the writer's knowledge the technology has not been thoroughly enough tested to prove the claims).
Combustion of coal would result in the volatilization of trace elements contained in the coal. Trace element concentrations in the various coal seams present on Tracts II and III have been presented in Chapter II (Table II-10); implications have been discussed in previous sections.
Land Use
A conversion plant and related facilities would cover some 1,000 acres of land. If a plant were sited in the valley of Sarpy Creek, the preempted land use would be primarily agricultural; wildlife habitat and recreational values also would be lost for the life of the facility.
